papers.title: Mercury (Hg): a relativistic $N$-body simulation for Horndeski gravity
papers.summary: We present Mercury, a relativistic $N$-body code for cosmological simulations in the $α$-basis formulation of Horndeski gravity. Mercury extends a particle-mesh scheme by incorporating the dynamics of the additional scalar degree of freedom and the corresponding modified Einstein equations, expressed in terms of the time-dependent functions $α_{\rm K}, α_{\rm B}, α_{\rm M}, α_{\rm T}$ and the effective Planck mass $M_*^2$. This generalises our previous implementation of Horndeski subclass models, namely $k$-essence and kinetic gravity braiding (KGB), to the general linear Horndeski $α$-basis. The code evolves the additional scalar degree of freedom and its effective stress--energy tensor alongside the nonlinear matter and metric fields, so that nonlinear structure formation sources the scalar-field evolution and feeds back on the gravitational potentials. Through its interface with hi_class, Mercury supports both phenomenological $α$-function parametrisations and covariant Horndeski theories; we demonstrate the latter using nKGB, the Cubic Galileon, and Brans--Dicke models. We validate the implementation against hi_class in the linear regime and recover the expected nonlinear $k$-essence and KGB limits. For the luminal Horndeski models considered here, we show how a running effective Planck mass generates gravitational slip through the scalar anisotropic stress and modifies the friction terms governing the vector and tensor metric perturbations. The evolution of $M_*^2$ also modifies the normalisation and scale dependence of the effective dark-energy density contrast, leaving a corresponding imprint on its power spectrum. The present framework provides an intermediate step towards nonlinear Horndeski simulations, in which nonlinear scalar self-interactions and screening effects can be incorporated consistently within the same relativistic framework.

papers.title: Ultrafast X-ray-induced dephasing of valence electrons
papers.summary: Diffract-before-destroy schemes for atomic-scale electron mapping assume that ultrashort X-ray pulses outrun radiation damage. Although atomic cores move over tens of femtoseconds, outer electrons respond much faster, compromising their locations. We test this limit in elemental silicon using broadband, energy-chirped X-ray pulses to encode time with few-femtosecond resolution. Comparing valence-sensitive structurally forbidden reflections with simultaneously measured core-dominated Bragg peaks reveals valence-bond dephasing on sub-20-fs timescales even at pulse energies where direct ionization effects are negligible. Our findings demonstrate that crystallography where outer electrons contribute substantially to Bragg peaks requires pulses shorter than today's standard $\sim50\,fs$ standard. They also establish a path to disentangle valence electron and lattice contributions to order and dynamics with hard X-rays, enabling studies across molecular biology, quantum matter and devices.

papers.title: Mutual information to all orders from modular flow: a replica-free approach
papers.summary: We derive an all-orders long-distance expansion of vacuum mutual information between two disjoint balls in generic $d$-dimensional CFTs. The derivation uses a novel radial sewing expansion of the joint vacuum density matrix, together with a modular response formula for relative entropy and the geometric modular flow of a single ball, without analytic continuation in replica number. The expansion coefficients are modular integrals of modular-flowed vacuum correlators. Our formula provides a systematic treatment of arbitrary multi-point sectors, and recovers known results on two-point sector derived from replica methods. The full two-point sector resums into a modular integral of the thermal partition function on $S^{d-1}$, with an effective temperature depending on ball configuration and modular time. We compute the expansion explicitly in CFTs. In two-dimensional Ising CFT, using analytic reductions and multidimensional numerical integration, we obtain the first ten radial orders in the long-distance expansion, which involve sphere correlators with up to twenty spin insertions. The truncated expansion agrees well with lattice data at finite separation, and approximately satisfies crossing symmetry. Analytic calculations also reproduce known expansion coefficients for 2d free compact boson at self-dual radius and its current sector, as well as for free scalars in higher dimensions.

papers.title: Inhomogeneous Synthetic Fluxes in Optical Lattices
papers.summary: Synthetic gauge fields in optical lattices are usually engineered to realize a uniform magnetic flux. Here, we propose a scheme to generate spatially inhomogeneous fluxes and demonstrate how such fluxes reshape the single-particle spectrum. Within Wannier--Stark-assisted tunneling, onsite modulation produces a plaquette flux that depends on the orientation of the static tilt, whereas laser-assisted tunneling (LAT) does not. Using LAT, two coherent Raman processes with different momentum transfers imprint a dimerized Peierls phase that alternates the flux between neighboring plaquettes of a square lattice while keeping the mean flux fixed. A bond-selective Raman phase extends the scheme to the kagome lattice, where a parameter $ξ$ redistributes the flux between triangles and hexagons at fixed flux per unit cell. The Hofstadter--Rammal spectrum of the bipartite square lattice retains chiral symmetry for all $ξ$, whereas the kagome lattice lacks this symmetry, and its flux periodicity and reflection symmetries survive only at special values of $ξ$. As $ξ$ is reduced, the anomalous Landau levels of the kagome singular flat band are compressed toward the flat-band energy and evolve into a degenerate zero-energy manifold at $ξ=0$ with compactly localized states. The dynamical structure factor, accessible through Bragg scattering, resolves this evolution as a Rydberg-like series of peaks whose spectral span tracks the width of the anomalous-level tower and vanishes as $ξ\to0$. We discuss the frequency resolution and temperature required for its observation.

papers.title: Internal friction and frequency-dependent conductivity in the bivariate site energy model for the mixed alkali effect in glasses
papers.summary: The mixed alkali effect is fundamental to understanding ion transport in glasses. It manifests itself in strong changes of various ionic transport properties when one type of ion is successively replaced by another type. Recently, we have developed a new theory of thermally activated hopping in bivariate random site energy landscapes that takes into account site occupation statistics according to generalized Fermi distributions and mixture kinetics in accordance with linear irreversible thermodynamics. The theory was successfully applied to predict the behavior of partial conductivities and their activation energies at low frequencies corresponding to the dc limit. Here we show that the theory is capable to capture the salient features of the mixed alkali effect observed in ac ion conductivities and in the peculiar behavior of the internal friction.

papers.title: The Virasoro Bootstrap: from the $c\sim1$ desert to coupled Potts
papers.summary: We develop a numerical conformal bootstrap for two-dimensional CFTs with $c>1$ based on Virasoro conformal blocks, computed with Zamolodchikov's recursion and optimal polynomial interpolation. As a first test we isolate an island around three decoupled Ising models. We then consider three 3-state Potts models coupled through their energy operators, a candidate irrational CFT. Mixed correlators isolate the decoupled theory in an island, and different gap assumptions, motivated by perturbation theory, yield a peninsula that contains the coupled fixed point but not the decoupled one. Finally, we explore the standard single-correlator bound on the lowest-dimension scalar primary in the OPE of two identical scalars. We find that for central charges just above $c=1$ the bound collapses over a wide range of external dimensions. This excludes any theory whose lightest scalar is absent from its own OPE and lies in this range, and supports the conjecture that no compact CFT exists in this region. We explain several features of these bounds analytically.

papers.title: Multiple windows of eigenstate-selective delocalization in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice
papers.summary: We investigate localization in a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattice with a real quasiperiodic onsite potential of strength $W$ and a staggered imaginary quasiperiodic modulation of strength $λ$. Using the inverse participation ratio (IPR), normalized participation ratio (NPR), fractal dimension $D_2$, transfer-matrix Lyapunov exponent, and wave-packet dynamics, we find a strongly non-monotonic and state-dependent response. At fixed $λ$, varying $W$ yields two distinct delocalization windows, whereas varying $λ$ at fixed $W$ produces a single re-entrant delocalization window. These regimes arise within selected eigenstate sectors, where localized states coexist with extended or critical states, leading to mobility-edge-like behavior. The corresponding suppression of the Lyapunov exponent and enhancement of the dynamical RMS spreading are consistent with the IPR, NPR, and $D_2$ results. Finite-size scaling confirms the persistence of the re-entrant features, while the complex-energy spectrum resolves their state-selective structure. The resulting phase boundaries delineate distinct localization regimes in the $(W,λ)$ plane. Our results show that the interplay between quasiperiodicity and a staggered non-Hermitian modulation sharing the same quasiperiodic spatial structure can generate re-entrant, state-dependent localization, with implications for localization and dynamics in non-Hermitian quasiperiodic lattices.

papers.title: An Intrinsically Gapless Topological Phase with Dipole Symmetry
papers.summary: We show that the boundary fractionalization familiar from gapped topological insulators can enforce bulk gaplessness in a dipole-conserving system. In a one-dimensional fermion model with charge conservation, dipole conservation, and particle-hole symmetry, we realize an intrinsically gapless symmetry-protected topological (igSPT) phase combining a dipolar Luttinger liquid with half-quantized boundary charges. This boundary structure obstructs a unique gapped bulk preserving these symmetries and lattice translation. Remarkably, the two charge-neutral edge configurations remain exactly degenerate even at finite size due to dipole conservation and particle-hole symmetry. The boundary fractionalization also manifests as shifted conformal towers in the dipole-resolved entanglement spectrum, reflecting distinct conformal boundary conditions of the Luttinger liquid. We support our analysis of the igSPT by studying exactly-solvable limits and performing DMRG computations, establishing its stability for a wide range of tuning parameters.

papers.title: The effects of an alternating bias on a single orbital spin impurity
papers.summary: Electron spin resonance with the scanning tunneling microscope (ESR-STM) enables coherent manipulation and detection of individual atomic spins with atomic-scale spatial resolution, yet the microscopic mechanism by which the radiofrequency (RF) bias drives the spin remains under debate. We study this problem using a Redfield quantum-master-equation framework in which the oscillating bias enters explicitly through the electronic reservoirs rather than through an effective time-dependent tunneling amplitude. In the semiclassical limit, the RF voltage periodically sweeps the system through its static transport landscape, so that the transport regime depends jointly on the DC bias and RF amplitude. When the RF trajectory approaches or crosses a charge transition, the damping-like torque (DLT) associated with spin-polarized charge transfer is strongly enhanced. By contrast, the field-like torque (FLT) induced by the exchange field remains finite deeper in the Coulomb-blockade (CB) regime because it originates from virtual charge fluctuations. The RF trajectory also averages strongly bias-dependent static quantities over a finite voltage range, smoothing features such as the Lamb shift near the charge thresholds. These results establish the RF amplitude as a control parameter not only for the strength of the ESR drive, but also for the transport regime and the ratio between FLT and DLT.

papers.title: Polariton tweezers
papers.summary: The non-invasive, deterministic manipulation of charge carriers remains a fundamental challenge in solid-state quantum technologies. Here, we demonstrate the concept of dynamic polariton tweezers capable of trapping and transporting electrons across a two-dimensional electron system via the long-range electrostatic potential of dipolar (d-) exciton-polaritons. By driving a semiconductor microcavity with a specifically engineered, non-collinear three-beam optical pump with TE-polarization, we synthesize a macroscopic polariton lattice with hexagonal symmetry. The spatially periodic field of this d-polariton condensate acts as a reconfigurable trapping landscape for the electrons. We show that introducing targeted frequency detunings between the continuous-wave pumps strictly breaks the spatiotemporal symmetry of the system, converting the stationary macroscopic interference pattern into a dynamically moving conveyor belt. By precisely customizing these frequency detunings, the entire lattice - along with the electrostatically trapped electrons - can be rigidly driven in any arbitrary in-plane direction. This precise phase-matching mechanism bypasses the need for a net kinetic momentum transfer, establishing a robust, optically controlled platform for the long-range routing of charged particles and topological defects in driven-dissipative quantum fluids.

papers.title: Cage-enforced i-wave altermagnetism in boron-carbon clathrates
papers.summary: The spin splitting of an altermagnet arises from a rotation that relates its two magnetic sublattices. In known cases it is fixed by the crystal structure. Here we show that guest-host frameworks separate the two roles. In the boron-carbon clathrates $M$B$_3$C$_3$ the ordered cage removes the translation between the two guest sites and enforces cubic $i$-wave altermagnetism, with six symmetry-enforced nodal planes, for any magnetic guest in the compensated state; strain retunes the class to $d$- or $g$-wave. We demonstrate the platform with GdB$_3$C$_3$: its compensated antiferromagnetic ground state is a narrow-gap semiconductor with spin splitting of 0.19 eV at the conduction-band edge, and its weakly pinned Néel vector switches the helicity-resolved optical response on and off according to the magnetic point group. Thermodynamic stability at high pressure and dynamical stability at ambient pressure indicate that it can be made by the route established for this family.

papers.title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
papers.summary: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

papers.title: Theory of the Ferroaxial Charge Density Wave in 1T-TiSe$_2$
papers.summary: Recent experiments using strain to probe the charge-density wave (CDW) of 1T-TiSe$_2$ have uncovered additional transitions and broken symmetries inside the CDW state. The elastocaloric effect reveals a second transition below $T_\mathrm{CDW}$, which elastoresistivity shows to be associated with ferroaxial order, breaking all vertical mirror symmetries while preserving inversion. In addition, at even lower temperatures, a diverging nematic susceptibility has been reported through elastoresistivity. In this work, we argue that this rich phenomenology cannot be explained by the standard $L_1^-$ CDW order parameter, and instead requires the existence of a secondary CDW order parameter. Based on symmetry, microscopic, and diffraction considerations, we propose this subleading CDW to have $L_2^-$ symmetry. By analyzing the Landau theory of coupled $L_1^-$ and $L_2^-$ orders in the presence of strain, we reproduce the phase boundaries observed in the elastocaloric measurements and the emergence of ferroaxial order below the CDW transition. Moreover, the model supports a third threefold-rotational symmetry breaking transition at lower temperatures, consistent with the reported divergence of the nematic susceptibility.

papers.title: Polarity-Programmed Topological Gating of Knotting in Spatially Patterned Active Polymers
papers.summary: Spatially patterned tangential activity provides a route to program polymer topology through both geometry and propulsion direction. We use Langevin-dynamics simulations of a flexible, self-avoiding linear polymer to determine how active-domain placement and independently assigned propulsion polarities control nonequilibrium knotting. Reversing the polarities of two terminal active blocks switches the steady state from a nearly always-knotted regime to effective knot suppression, changing the knotting probability by more than three orders of magnitude despite identical active-block positions and activity magnitude. Across symmetric terminal two-block architectures, we further identify an approximate zero-one-two free-end-alignment rule: zero, one, and two free-end-aligned active blocks correspond, respectively, to suppressed, intermediate, and high-knotting states. A two-state kinetic decomposition shows that the conditional knot-formation rate changes only by about threefold under polarity reversal, whereas the mean knot lifetime changes by several orders of magnitude, demonstrating that knot survival and passive-region storage dominate the polarity-controlled switch. Block placement provides an additional geometrical gate: moving an active domain from the chain interior to a terminal region strongly enhances both knot formation and survival. Knot-center residence, knotted-arc distributions, and episode-resolved kymographs reveal formation near free-end-aligned active blocks, directed contour migration, tightening, and long-lived retention in passive regions. Together, these results support a source-conveyor-reservoir-sink mechanism in which signed polarity and spatial activity patterning control whether knots are generated, transported, stored, or rapidly lost, providing a route to programmable topological states in nonequilibrium active polymers.

papers.title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
papers.summary: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.

papers.title: Exceptional Points and Optimized Encoding in Qubit Stabilizer Codes
papers.summary: Continuous blind stabilizer measurements turn stabilizer codes into a Liouvillian spectral problem in which Hamiltonian terms compete with dissipative error channels. We show that this competition generically enables Liouvillian exceptional points, whose occurrence at weak error rates is constrained by the code distance. Exceptional points are detrimental in this regime of error correction as they maximize the decay rate of encoded coherences. We then optimize the encoding of the logical qubit using the eigenmodes of the Lindblad operator. This phase-optimized encoding cancels the linear short-time decay of logical qubit coherences. We apply this encoding to the [[5,1,3]] code and demonstrate that it outperforms naive encoding methods near the exceptional point, improves the fidelity of a logical $π$ rotation and remains effective in the presence of additional weak error channels.

papers.title: Aberration stabilized light bullets in normal dispersion injected Kerr resonators
papers.summary: We investigate three-dimensional light bullets (LBs) in an optically injected, vertically emitting Kerr-Gires-Tournois interferometer operating in the normal dispersion regime. In the uniform field limit, the dynamics is governed by a generalized Lugiato-Lefever equation with third-order dispersion, paraxial diffraction, and fourth-order diffraction, stemming from lens and mirror aberrations close to the self-imaging condition. Using direct numerical simulations, we show that without aberration only transversely drifting, tilted multi-peak localized states (LSs) are stable in two dimensions, whereas no stable LBs exist in three dimensions. However, a small negative spherical aberration stabilizes a rich multistable family of two-dimensional LSs, including straight and tilted multi-peak LSs, oscillating states, and complex bound states, which persist even for negative paraxial diffraction. We identify an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation followed by a homoclinic transition toward tilted states, accompanied by hysteresis. Finally, we demonstrate that stable straight and tilted LBs exist in three dimensions in the presence of aberration, the latter forming a continuous family parametrized by the transverse tilt direction.

papers.title: Local and itinerant orbital contributions to the gyromagnetic response of paramagnetic metals
papers.summary: Orbitronics exploits orbital angular momentum to generate and manipulate angular-momentum currents for controlling magnetisation, offering new approaches to magnetic memory and logic. A quantitative description of this process requires establishing how orbital angular momentum contributes to magnetic moments and, consequently, to the gyromagnetic response that governs magnetisation dynamics. Here, we present a first-principles framework for calculating the effective gyromagnetic tensor (g') of paramagnetic metals, consistently incorporating local and itinerant orbital contributions, spin-orbit coupling, and both state- and occupation-change effects. Applying the framework to V and Pt, we find that orbital paramagnetic responses are comparable to or larger than spin contributions and substantially modify g' from the free-electron value. The atom-centered approximation can underestimate the orbital response by approximately a factor of two, while neglecting occupation changes produces significant errors in the calculated g'. Our calculated g' values for V and Pt agree with experiment, while their pronounced dependence on band filling reveals a route to engineering angular-momentum responses through electronic-structure control. The results establish the modern theory of orbital magnetism as an essential ingredient for describing gyromagnetic response and provide a framework for identifying materials with enhanced orbital functionalities.

papers.title: Amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line
papers.summary: Propagating spin waves have emerged as promising candidates for signal processing and information transmission. We present a theoretical investigation of the generation, propagation and collection of spin-wave wave packets in micrometer-wide magnetic conduits, highlighting their potential for analogue frequency demultiplexing in space and time. We clarify the roles of the excitation duration and of the spin wave dispersion relation, as well as the influence of the spin-wave linewidth in setting the spatio-temporal evolution of propagating spin-wave wavepackets excited by Gaussian field pulses. We issue rules for the spatio-temporal separation of wavepackets that carry different frequencies. We finally propose an amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line of 60x5 $μ$m$^2$ footprint.

papers.title: Symmetry breaking from conformality loss on holographic Rényi defects
papers.summary: The Rényi entropies of a ball are computed by a conformal defect, the Rényi defect, dual in holography to a hyperbolic black hole. At an index $n_*$ its charged operator merges with its alternate-quantization partner, and the defect loses conformality. Beyond $n_*$ it flows with no source to a conformal defect that breaks the U(1) symmetry; below $n_*$ that defect needs a symmetry-breaking source, so at large $N$, conformality loss makes the breaking spontaneous. The scalar hair beyond $n_*$, expected to break the symmetries of hyperbolic space, thus preserves them outside a thin layer at the entangling surface, as conformal symmetry requires. The region outside the layer sets the universal term of the Rényi entropy. We demonstrate the mechanism in the probe Abelian Higgs model in AdS$_5$ at the Bogomolny point, where the saddles are in closed form and numerical methods confirm the flows. On a sphere we prove that a positive source-free flow exists exactly when $n>n_*$ and the sphere is large enough; it is then unique and ends at the symmetry-breaking defect. The mechanism needs a scalar mass in a finite window, and for potentials attractive at small amplitude, the symmetry can break before conformality is lost. For operators of low enough dimension, already the second Rényi entropy lies beyond the merger. Classical backreaction does not move the merger at any order; we argue that away from $n_*$ the flows persist at first order.

papers.title: Acoustic damping limits superfluid helium as a thermal bath for mechanical resonators
papers.summary: Thermalization is a persistent problem for cryogenic mechanical resonators. The weak supports used to obtain high mechanical quality factors are also poor thermal links, while the optical or microwave fields used for readout and control can heat the resonator above the cryostat temperature. Superfluid helium is therefore an appealing exchange medium: it has excellent low-temperature thermal transport and an inviscid superfluid component, suggesting cooling of mechanical devices without the damping associated with an ordinary fluid. Here we test this idea by immersing a \qty{250}{\micro\meter}-diameter yttrium iron garnet sphere in liquid \textsuperscript{4}He and reading out a \(\sim\qty{12.47}{\mega\hertz}\) mechanical mode using cavity magnomechanics. The mechanical linewidth increases from \qty{6.1}{\hertz} in vacuum to \qty{9.1}{\kilo\hertz} after filling the cavity with liquid helium in the normal state, and reaches \qty{17.5}{\kilo\hertz} deep in the superfluid at \qty{84}{\milli\kelvin}. Thus the mechanical quality factor is reduced by more than three orders of magnitude, and crossing into the superfluid does not recover low dissipation. At the same time, the magnon linewidth remains strongly dependent on microwave power at the lowest temperatures, showing that the sphere is not perfectly anchored to the cryostat despite the large mechanical damping. The result follows from acoustic radiation: the surface motion of the sphere efficiently launches gapless longitudinal sound into the liquid, and a radiation-impedance estimate gives a linewidth of order \qty{25}{\kilo\hertz}. Superfluid helium is therefore not a low-loss thermal bath for mechanical modes that efficiently radiate compression waves. Shear motion, on the other hand, may provide a route around this limitation.

papers.title: Piezogyration and elastogyration in ternary chalcopyrites from first principles
papers.summary: Natural optical activity arises from the spatial dispersion of the optical response and is described by the rank-two gyration pseudotensor. Its dependence on mechanical stress and strain, quantified by the piezogyration and elastogyration tensors, respectively, has been investigated experimentally for decades. However, a systematic first-principles description of these effects remains largely unexplored. Here we present a first-principles methodology to compute the full piezogyration and elastogyration tensors, and apply it to a set of representative ternary chalcopyrite crystals. The gyration of the unstrained crystal turns out to be a poor predictor of the magnitude of the elastogyration response, which we find to be a property inherited from their parent zinc-blende structures. The elastic compliance tensor further shapes the piezogyration response, with particularly pronounced effects in AgGaS$_2$, a well-known achiral yet optically active crystal. Finally, we explore strain-induced chirality through the trace of the gyration tensor, the only pseudoscalar contribution to the natural optical activity that is linear in the tensor components and encodes information about chirality.

papers.title: Rate-selective synchronization in switching networks: when timing meets structure
papers.summary: Switching networks arise across physics, biology, and engineering, where interactions turn on and off due to communication limits, control protocols, failures, or scheduling. Most synchronization theory for switching networks of continuous-time oscillators relies on the fast-switching approximation, yet many systems operate outside this regime, where switching can produce unexpected and counterintuitive collective dynamics. We develop the first analytical framework for synchronization in non-fast-switching networks of saddle-focus continuous-time oscillators. Using Rössler and piecewise-smooth systems as canonical examples, we leverage a structural property of saddle-focus oscillators to reduce the variational dynamics to a linear system with constant coefficients, enabling a Floquet-theoretic stability characterization under periodic switching. The analysis identifies explicit switching intervals that stabilize synchronization even when neither switching mode nor the corresponding average system supports synchronization in isolation, thereby revealing the mechanism underlying the emergence of "windows of opportunity" at intermediate switching rates. We further derive a switching-dependent master stability function linking the network Laplacian spectrum to the switching rate. The master stability function provides two complementary routes to inducing or preserving synchronization: adjusting the switching schedule for a fixed network or adapting the network spectrum to a prescribed schedule through our constructive edge-pruning or edge-augmentation algorithms. These results provide a rigorous basis for understanding and leveraging intermediate-rate switching in the design and control of evolving networks.

papers.title: Functional Dimensional Regularization for the Lee-Yang Model
papers.summary: We apply functional dimensional regularization (FDR) to the Lee-Yang universality class, a paradigmatic non-unitary theory, and compute its main critical exponents across the dimension range $3\leq d\leq 6$. By combining a second-order derivative expansion with polynomial field expansions, we obtain results that are compatible with resummed $\varepsilon$-expansion as well as with state-of-the-art estimates from Conformal Bootstrap and Fuzzy Sphere techniques. This demonstrates that, in the context of non-unitary theories, FDR retains the efficiency and rapid convergence to accurate critical exponents already observed in the Ising and O(N) cases.

papers.title: Electron--phonon cooling noise in monolayer and bilayer graphene
papers.summary: We study the electron--phonon heat-current fluctuations in monolayer and Bernal bilayer graphene coupled to longitudinal acoustic phonons. To do this, we construct a symmetric heat-current operator and evaluate the non-equilibrium current--current correlator at finite frequency for unequal electron and phonon temperatures. The heat-current vertices then involve the probe energy combined with twice the phonon energy, and the nonequilibrium spectral density must be calculated directly rather than inferred from a dynamic thermal fluctuation--dissipation relation. Further, we obtain full analytical expressions in the Bloch--Grüneisen (BG) and Equipartition (EP) regimes, derive their low-frequency limits, and compare them with a complete doped-intraband on-shell calculations for monolayer graphene. The numerical results connect the two temperature regimes and show how finite-frequency noise changes out of equilibrium. For representative parameters, the corrections become percent-level in the upper-gigahertz to sub-terahertz range. It is worth mentioning that in equilibrium, the results satisfy the zero-frequency thermal fluctuation--dissipation relation(FDT) and reproduce the well established cooling-power and thermal-conductance laws.

papers.title: Magnetic field as a tuning knob for edge mode interaction in integer quantum Hall interferometers
papers.summary: The quantum Hall interferometer has been shown to be a powerful tool for probing both the nature of the chiral modes present at the edges of these systems and the interactions between them. Strong inter-edge mode interactions can lead the system into a regime where the period of the interferometer signal corresponds to an insertion of a half-quantum flux h/2e, rather than the standard flux quantum h/e. Using a highly tunable bilayer graphene device, we are able to measure the prevalence of both the h/e-period and the doubled-frequency regimes as a function of magnetic field, providing insight into the microscopic nature of the doubling mechanism. Furthermore, we are able to push our device to a regime where double-frequency oscillations coexist with a superimposed period-h/e pattern associated with the inner chiral modes farther from the edge. We argue that this regime has a natural interpretation in a picture of the frequency doubling being caused by strong capacitive couplings between the edge modes.

papers.title: From photons to fractons: Casimir effect in higher-rank electrodynamics and its fractonic branch
papers.summary: The Casimir effect probes the modes that can propagate between boundaries. This makes it useful for fracton gauge theories, where restricted mobility follows from the simultaneous conservation of charge and dipole moment and changes the physical sector of the theory. We compare ordinary Maxwell electrodynamics with a Lorentz-covariant higher-rank theory of a symmetric tensor gauge field and with the scalar-charge fractonic branch selected from it by a preferred timelike background. The comparison shows why the distinction matters. In the full covariant theory, the Euclidean slab problem contains three independently propagating Maxwell-like modes and two coupled vector sectors that do not reduce to independent ordinary modes. Their boundary determinants are well defined, but a Lorentzian analysis shows that the vector sector has an unbounded Hamiltonian, so these determinants do not describe the vacuum energy of a stable fractonic phase. On the fractonic branch, the Gauss constraint removes that vector sector and leaves three stable massless modes: two transverse-traceless tensor modes and one scalar trace mode. For ideal reflectors, the physical Casimir energy is therefore 3/2 of the corresponding Maxwell result, for both equal and complementary boundary conditions. The calculation isolates the effect of the fractonic restriction on the radiative spectrum and clarifies which features of the full higher-rank boundary problem survive in the physical fracton sector.

papers.title: When will androids outnumber humans?
papers.summary: Humanoid robots are increasingly discussed not only as machines but also as a potential technological population. We develop a nonlinear population-dynamical framework to examine their possible diffusion relative to humans, without assuming that large-scale adoption or numerical crossover is inevitable. The human population $H(t)$ is calibrated to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 median trajectory. The android population $A(t)$ is represented through the normalized stock $a=A/A_s$. A conventional, human-organized manufacturing and adoption channel is calibrated to a conditional scenario spanning approximately $10^4$ humanoids in 2025 to $10^9$ in 2050 and follows $\dot a=(q_M+r_Ma)\exp(K_Ma^γ)$. We separately introduce a hypothetical autonomous channel in which installed androids contribute materially to producing additional androids. Under the minimal canonical TZ closure, the corresponding production--feedback number is $\mathcal{P}(a)=(r_A/δ_A)\exp(K_Ra)$, where $r_A$ is the gross robot-mediated production coefficient, $δ_A$ the retirement rate, and $K_R$ the autonomous feedback parameter. This channel is locally self-amplifying if and only if $\mathcal{P}>1$, whereas numerical human--android parity, $A=H$, is a separate cumulative condition. Global uncertainty analysis shows that crossover dates remain strongly scenario-dependent, while the production--feedback threshold is more robust. An extreme early-autonomy stress test can produce parity by 2050, but this represents a conditional dynamical boundary rather than a technological forecast.

papers.title: Establishing Néel order in the square-lattice antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model: a bootstrap proof
papers.summary: Rigorously establishing spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) in the thermodynamic limit is generally challenging. This is exemplified by the two-dimensional (2D) $S = 1/2$ antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model where the existence of Néel order is not rigorously established despite overwhelming evidence from a variety of methods. We show that a bootstrap approach can be used to rigorously establish SSB and use it to prove the existence of Néel order in the 2D $S = 1/2$ XXZ model by deriving a strictly positive lower bound on the Néel order parameter for a set of discrete values of the anisotropy parameter $Δ$ in the range $[0,2]$ including the isotropic (Heisenberg) point $Δ= 1$. Our approach employs a generalization of the Kennedy--Lieb--Shastry inequalities, which use an infrared bound to reduce the existence of long-range order to bounds on certain finite-distance correlators. We compute these bounds for all sufficiently large systems with periodic boundary conditions using the bootstrap. An important ingredient in our proof is a novel method for obtaining exactly certified variational upper bounds on the energy density in the thermodynamic limit from matrix product states. Our approach can be readily generalized to other local lattice models for which infrared susceptibility bounds can be obtained.

papers.title: Mechano-chemical control of enzymatic activity in crowded environments
papers.summary: Macromolecular crowding has long been known to alter biochemical equilibria and enzyme kinetics, with reported catalytic activities that may increase, decrease, or vary non-monotonically with crowder concentration. Classical Michaelis--Menten kinetics does not by itself identify which of these responses should occur for a conformationally active enzyme. Here, we develop a minimal non-equilibrium mechano-chemical theory for a fueled enzyme embedded in a bath of passive crowders and uncover a fluctuation-induced effective force dipole acting on the enzyme subunits, akin to a generalized form of dispersion or depletion interaction. Since the preferred conformation of the model enzyme varies through the catalytic cycle, the fluctuation-induced mechanical load affects the relevant kinetic activation barriers and is sufficient to produce both monotonic inhibition and non-monotonic modification of turnover. The framework provides a thermodynamically consistent route for linking crowded environments to catalytic currents, suggesting how mechanical design principles could be leveraged to control enzymatic pathways.

papers.title: Microscopic Origin of the Equation of Motion for Open Thermodynamic Systems
papers.summary: In my previous work (arXiv:2609.07810) \cite{Aydiner_2026}, I derived a second-order equation of motion for open thermodynamic systems from the First Law of Thermodynamics and established its dynamical equivalence with mechanical oscillators and electrical RLC circuits. In the present study, I independently recover the same mathematical structure of the equation of motion from a mesoscopic model of particle transfer between two reservoirs connected by a channel. Starting from collective momentum balance, particle conservation, and reservoir chemical-potential response, I derive the inertial--dissipative--restoring dynamics and obtain explicit expressions for its effective coefficients in terms of the physical parameters of the system. The resulting equation predicts distinct damping regimes, characteristic relaxation time scales, and resonance under periodic driving. The natural frequency and resonance conditions are explicitly determined by the physical parameters of the particle-transfer system. In the slow-transport limit, the model recovers the conventional Onsager-type linear flux--force relation. The independent emergence of the same dynamical structure from two distinct physical approaches provides theoretical support for the previously proposed thermodynamic equation of motion. By identifying the physical mechanisms underlying its effective coefficients, the present study strengthens the physical foundations of the proposed framework and supports the possibility of describing open thermodynamic systems within a common dynamical framework shared with mechanical and electrical systems.

papers.title: Spin SYK-dot chains: entanglement bound and resource estimates towards a quantum advantage
papers.summary: Ground states of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK)-type models are volume-law entangled, which makes them costly both for tensor networks and for quantum hardware simulations. Thus, it remains unclear where quantum hardware could outperform classical simulation of such models. In this work, we study a spin SYK-dot chain, in which q dense SYK dots of p qubits are joined by single ZZ bonds of strength K. The entanglement across any cut is then bounded by floor(p/2) ln 2 plus the inter-dot entanglement, and the two-qubit depth of one Trotter step is set by p alone. A resource estimate shows that a quantum advantage for the ground state could appear only for dots of about 15 to 21 qubits or more. There, a single Trotter step already requires two-qubit error rates of order 10^{-6}, beyond the reach of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. We test the assumptions of this estimate with an imaginary-time matrix product state (MPS) that applies each dot as one block. It agrees with exact diagonalisation at (p, q) = (6, 2). At (5, 2), a variational circuit with the same dot-plus-link layout comes within 3.6% of the exact energy, and noisy simulations show that its fidelity decays as assumed in the resource estimate. At (8, 5), i.e., N = 40 qubits, the energy converges at bond dimension chi = 768, far below the exact value 2^20, and the inter-dot entanglement stays small and is set mainly by K. Out-of-time-order correlators across the links decay on a time scale that shrinks rapidly with |K|. Thus, the dot size p and the inter-dot coupling K together set the entanglement of the chain, and with it where a quantum advantage could appear.

papers.title: Universality and Emergent Classicality in Krylov Space
papers.summary: Krylov complexity grows linearly at late times for many systems. In this regime, we give a general spectral formula for the leading growth coefficients of Krylov complexity and its higher moments, without requiring detailed knowledge of the Lanczos coefficients. For states with a narrow energy distribution compared to the bandwidth, dynamics in the Krylov basis resembles motion along a classical trajectory. We demonstrate our results for the critical XY chain and double-scaled SYK. For the latter, we compute the leading late-time behavior of the chord-number moments through one-loop order.

papers.title: Density and Current Fluctuations for Run-and-Tumble Particles With and Without Interactions
papers.summary: We study density and current fluctuations in a one-dimensional gas of run-and-tumble particles (RTPs), whose intrinsic velocities switch between two opposite values at a constant rate. We consider particles with and without pair interactions, including regularized Riesz gases, and also obtain corresponding results for Brownian particles. By linearizing the Dean-Kawasaki (DK) equations around a homogeneous stationary state, we compute density correlations and the variance of the integrated current through the origin. For repulsive Riesz interactions decaying as $1/|x|^s$ with $s>0$, this variance grows at long times as $t^{1/2}$ for $s>1$, but as $t^{s/(1+s)}$ for $0<s<1$. Starting from the same DK description, but retaining the Poisson statistics of direction reversals, we derive a macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) for RTPs with smooth pair interaction potential, which allows to compute the large time large deviation of the time integrated current. We show that, in the absence of interactions, the MFT saddle point equations can be solved explicitly using a generalized Cole-Hopf transform. This allows to recover and generalize previous results for the current distribution obtained by microscopic calculations, for RTPs with annealed or quenched step initial conditions. Beyond these distributions, MFT allows to compute the optimal density histories producing a prescribed current through the origin. We find that these density profiles, for both RTPs and Brownian particles, exhibit a nontrivial space-time structure. We also study stationary current fluctuations on an interval connected to reservoirs. Finally, we analyze the MFT equations perturbatively in the interaction. In both the infinite-line and reservoir geometries, we obtain explicit first-order corrections to the current generating functions for short-range interacting RTPs and Brownian particles.

papers.title: Pressure-correlation phase diagram unraveling quantum phase transitions in altermagnetic $ε$-FeOOH and realization of piezo-anomalous Hall effect
papers.summary: We establish a pressure-correlation phase diagram that yields multiple pressure-tunable quantum phase transitions in iron oxyhydroxide ($ε$-FeOOH) across three critical pressures, $P_{c1}>P_{c2}>P_{c3}$. The transitions arise from the competition among electron-correlation, crystal-field, and Hund's coupling. First-principles calculations reveal that the earlier reported high-spin (HS) to low-spin (LS) crossover at correlation-sensitive $P_{c1}$ is accompanied by a transition from charge-transfer to Mott insulating (CTI-MI) phase, and a change in the spin-quantization axis (SQA) from $\hat{y}$ to $\hat{x}$. The HS-LS crossover and CTI-MI transition is driven by the simultaneous increase in crystal-field splitting and decrease in Hund's coupling. The critical pressure $P_{c2}$ governing the structural transition from centrosymmetric $Pnnm$ phase to noncentrosymmetric $P2_1nm$ phase is found to be independent of electron-correlation. When correlation is strong, a third critical pressure ($P_{c3}$) emerges in the lower-pressure regime of the phase diagram. Validating the recent experimental observation, $P_{c3}$ is responsible for changing the SQA from $\hat{z}$ to $\hat{y}$. By exhibiting altermagnetism in both $P2_1nm$ and $Pnnm$ phases and possessing finite anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) only for SQA along $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$, $ε$-FeOOH enables a unique piezo-anomalous Hall effect where one can switch on the AHC at a lower pressure and change its direction at a higher pressure.

papers.title: A Topology-Based Approach to Representative Volume Element Assessment in Solid Oxide Cell Anodes Using Large Volume Tomography and Persistent Homology
papers.summary: Determining the representative volume element is essential for establishing statistically meaningful microstructure-property relationships. Conventional approaches rely on the convergence of selected geometric descriptors, which may yield different estimates of the representative volume. Here, we propose a topology-based framework for assessing the representative scale of a nickel-yttria-stabilized zirconia solid oxide cell anode reconstructed using plasma focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (121.8 um x 83.97 um x 45.99 um). Persistent homology was used to characterize the pore network, and normalized persistence images of subvolumes were compared with those of the largest available reference volume using the L1 distance. This provides a continuous measure of topological similarity across observation scales, rather than defining representativeness through a single convergence threshold. The topological distance decreases with increasing volume and is described by empirical exponential models over the investigated range (R2 in [0.972, 0.983]). Comparison with porosity and specific surface area highlights differences in the scale-dependent behavior of geometric and topological descriptors. The framework was also tested on three independent synthetic realizations, demonstrating its potential for quantitative assessment of topological similarity in porous microstructures.

papers.title: Enforced Gaplessness by Combining Non-Anomalous Symmetries
papers.summary: Symmetry-enforced gaplessness is a phenomenon in which a quantum system is forced to be gapless due to its global symmetry. Previous works have mainly focused on anomalous symmetries. Another approach, using symmetry spans, which specify two embeddings of a common symmetry into two larger symmetries, was proposed by the authors. In this work, we show that a symmetry span can enforce gaplessness even when both larger symmetries are invertible and non-anomalous: each alone admits a trivially gapped phase, but because the embeddings differ by a twist associated with a symmetry-protected topological phase, the symmetry they generate admits no gapped phase with finitely many ground states. We present such a span of a finite group and $\mathrm{U}(1)^2$ in 1+1 dimensions, with continuum realizations and a lattice Hamiltonian, with a finite-dimensional local Hilbert space and finitely many parameters, that is gapless in any region of its parameter space. We also discuss a 2+1-dimensional example and spans of only finite symmetries.

papers.title: Characterisation of surface layers formed on plasma-facing components in controlled fusion devices: Role of heavy ion elastic recoil detection
papers.summary: Wall components retrieved from the TEXTOR tokamak after tracer experiments with nitrogen-15 and molybdenum hexafluoride (MoF6) injection were studied to determine deposition patterns and, by this, to conclude on material migration. Toroidal limiter tiles made of carbon fibre composites and fine grain graphite were examined using time-of-flight heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis. Molybdenum deposition patterns indicated migration based on erosion and prompt re-deposition. Nitrogen-15 was trapped together with the deposited molybdenum. Some information on the depth distribution of species in the top 400 nm layer of the limiters was obtained; however surface roughness of the samples strongly limited resolution. In the case of molybdenum, the largest concentration was found in the 100 nm outermost layer, whereas fluorine and nitrogen-15 displayed more irregular profiles. Other species, besides deuterium fuel and carbon-12, were also identified: boron-10 and boron-11 originating from boronisations, carbon-13 from earlier tracer experiments, nitrogen-14 from plasma edge cooling and metals eroded from the Inconel wall.

papers.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
papers.summary: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

papers.title: A combined segmented anode gas ionization chamber and time-of-flight detector for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis
papers.summary: A dedicated detector system for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis at the Tandem Laboratory of Uppsala University is presented. Benefits of combining a time-of-flight measurement with a segmented anode gas ionization chamber are demonstrated. The capability of ion species identification is improved with the present system, compared to that obtained when using a single solid state silicon detector for the full ion energy signal. The system enables separation of light elements, up to Neon, based on atomic number while signals from heavy elements such as molybdenum and tungsten are separated based on mass, to a sample depth on the order of one micrometer. The performance of the system is discussed and a selection of material analysis applications is given. Plasma-facing materials from fusion experiments, in particular metal mirrors, are used as a main example for the discussion. Marker experiments using nitrogen-15 or oxygen-18 are specific cases for which the described improved species separation and sensitivity are required. Resilience to radiation damage and significantly improved energy resolution for heavy elements at low energies are additional benefits of the gas ionization chamber over a solid state detector based system.

papers.title: Writing with Near-Field: towards Atomic Resolution in Material Processing
papers.summary: Direct laser writing with ultra-short pulses is the most flexible route to two- and three-dimensional (2D/3D) material modification, yet its resolution is judged against the optical diffraction limit. This review argues the opposite: the finest, most reproducible modifications come not from shortening the wavelength but from localising the absorber. Through the threshold effect and a transient epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) state - the dielectric-to-metal (Die-Met) state of the excited solid - the deposited energy is confined to a dipole-like nano-seed whose near-field intensity falls as r^-6 (ideal point dipole). The localisation is thus set by the seed size, not the focal wavelength, and the final feature is shaped by the material response: post-pulse heat flow, cavitation and quenching. We show that polarisation controls the anisotropy of deposition: the quasi-static near-field and interface boundary conditions select the writing direction and the modification orientation, down to a single defect. We survey energy-deposition mechanisms from 100 nm to the single-nanometer scale and link them to working engineering: stitch-free large-area patterning and record aspect-ratio (10^3-10^4) dicing and wafering of transparent crystals. Finally, we conjecture guided volumetric deposition, in which laser-inscribed lossy nano-seeds act as antennas that let cavity microwaves anneal the modified nano-volumes from within, as a 2.45 GHz oven heats food through water-dipole absorption. Throughout, atomic resolution is used in a quantum-confined sense and denotes a direction of travel: 10-20 nm features are demonstrated, while deterministic single-defect and single-bond modification remain goals. The thesis is that ultrafast direct write beats diffraction-limited intuition because the material itself forms a transient nanoscale absorber whose near-field and boundary conditions govern energy deposition.

papers.title: Exact fermionic matrix elements from the Bethe-ansatz solution of the Richardson-Gaudin model
papers.summary: We introduce an effective Hamiltonian description of mesoscopic superconducting systems based on the Bethe-ansatz solution of the Richardson--Gaudin model. Our central result is a compact determinant formula for the matrix elements of fermionic creation and annihilation operators, expressed entirely in terms of eigenvalue-based variables. This formula allows single-electron tunneling terms to be represented directly in the eigenbasis of the Richardson--Gaudin model, extending the eigenvalue-based framework beyond overlaps and previously known form factors. As a benchmark, we apply the method to a superconducting Anderson impurity model comprising a quantum dot coupled to an ultrasmall superconducting grain. The resulting low-energy description, formulated naturally in the canonical ensemble, captures even-odd effects, subgap excitations, and quantum-dot physics. The same framework gives access to observables not previously computed for such grain-dot systems in the canonical ensemble, such as the fixed-particle-number optical conductivity and flux-tunable spectra.

papers.title: Synchronization and Spatiotemporal Phases in Driven Precessing Domain Walls
papers.summary: The dynamics of extended magnetic domain walls driven by constant and alternating magnetic fields are studied using a collective coordinate $u$-$φ$ model. While purely constant-field driven systems exhibit deterministic spatiotemporal chaos and roughening, the alternating component can lock the precessional frequency via Shapiro-like steps. Using linear stability analysis and Floquet theory, the phase boundaries of stable, synchronized flat wall states are mapped. By studying the nonlinear dynamics of the extended system, a rich phase diagram is identified, composed of five dynamical regimes characterized by the combination of domain wall spatial order (flat, rough, or periodic) and domain wall precession temporal order (pinned, synchronized, or unsynchronized). Notably, the macroscopic temporal order of the synchronized phases can lead to a flat domain wall or to a periodic structure dominated by a narrow band of linearly unstable modes, both with coherent precession of the domain wall magnetization, while unsynchronized phases can be flat, with coherent precession, or rough with spatiotemporal chaos and incoherent precession.

papers.title: Ultrafast Polar Topology Reversal via THz-Driven Inertial Switching
papers.summary: Topological polar structures in ferroelectric heterostructures offer functional states beyond ordinary domains. As polarization reversal underpins ferroelectric devices, switching between degenerate topological variants, which we refer to as topology reversal, would greatly expand the ways to control polar textures. However, polar topology reversal is challenging because it requires coordinated flipping of oppositely oriented local polarizations, a process not naturally driven by a uniform electric field. Using a multiscale modeling approach, we show that polar topology can be stabilized and reversed in a simple Pt/PbTiO$_3$/Pt nanocapacitor. Electrode-controlled boundary conditions drive tetragonal PbTiO$_3$ into competing orthorhombic- and rhombohedral-like polarization states, which form building blocks for diverse topological structures, including vortex arrays, skyrmion lattices, dipole spirals, and dipole waves. We further show that the same out-of-plane THz pulse can reversibly switch a double-$\mathbf q$ dipole wave between degenerate topological variants within a few picoseconds, while preserving its spatial modulation. This process is enabled by damping-assisted inertial switching, in which the THz pulse injects energy to drive large-angle polarization rotation across shallow barriers, while dissipation removes excess energy and traps the system in the reversed state. These results establish ferroelectric nanocapacitors as a simple platform for programmable polar topology and low-power, THz-speed control through dissipative dynamics.

papers.title: The normal approximation to macroscopic dynamical fluctuations
papers.summary: Under local detailed balance, the Lagrangian of macroscopic dynamical fluctuations has a canonical structure: its time-antisymmetric part is the entropy flux, and its time-symmetric part is a Legendre pair of kinetic and dissipation functions. We show what survives of that structure for normal (Gaussian) fluctuations around a nonequilibrium steady state. The quadratic Lagrangian keeps the canonical form, with the Hessian of the dissipation function as noise matrix. However, the force on the fluctuations differs from the linearized thermodynamic force by a term proportional to the driving and to the state dependence of the dynamical activity, so that local detailed balance is violated at the Gaussian level. Nevertheless, the Gaussian dynamics is gradient flow for the quadratic part of the nonequilibrium entropy, around an emergent nondissipative current. Finally, we show which parts of the Lagrangian can be reconstructed from measured Gaussian fluctuations.

papers.title: Hidden variable $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological order in a bilayer kagomé antiferromagnet
papers.summary: Topological orders in realistic systems are quite rare, raising one fundamental question of whether they might be harbored with hidden degrees of freedom rather than directly exposed in conventional spins or electrons. We here propose a set of hidden variables and their effective interactions in a bilayer kagomé antiferromagnet. By properly organizing four local states of the spin dimer into two pseudospin-$1/2$ variables ($\boldsymbolτ$ and $\boldsymbolμ$), we identify a regime where an effective Balents-Fisher-Girvin model emerges, realizing a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological order in the hidden $\boldsymbolτ$ sector while the auxiliary $\boldsymbolμ$ sector remains a trivial paramagnet. This hidden nature drastically alters the experimental manifestations. Physical spins map to composite objects, typically convolving fractionalized anyon continua with non-topological magnon excitations. Nevertheless, specific symmetry-selected channels, such as the longitudinal intralayer response, exclusively reveal the bare two-vison continuum without collective-mode dressing. Our findings demonstrate that the topological order could be buried in certain hidden and emergent degrees of freedom, pointing to a promising pathway for seeking elusive topological states disguised within hidden internal degrees of freedom.

papers.title: Noise-resilient collective order through temporal memory in self-propelled particles
papers.summary: Temporal memory can stabilise collective motion by filtering noisy local observations, but persistent information can also impede adaptation when the collective state changes. We investigate this competition in Vicsek-type systems using two distinct alignment rules: a finite buffer of past observations and a recursive update of an internal directional state. In both models, increasing effective memory shifts the loss of polar order to stronger noise and can restore ordered motion under conditions for which the corresponding memoryless Vicsek model is disordered. The stationary responses of the two models show an approximate correspondence when parameterised by a kernel-based effective memory, consistent with temporal averaging playing a common role in their ordering behaviour rather than from the details of the memory implementation. Their transient dynamics, however, are not determined by effective memory alone. Following a collective perturbation, recovery is fastest at an intermediate memory depth and becomes slower when outdated observations are retained too strongly. Temporal integration therefore produces a trade-off: deeper memory improves noise resilience, whereas excessive persistence reduces responsiveness. These results identify memory depth as a control parameter that separates the optimisation of stationary order from that of dynamical recovery in noisy active systems.

papers.title: Emergent stigmergy and pheromone-guided decisions in a foraging collective
papers.summary: Ants in a colony forage and recruit other nest-mates for cooperative transport of food through stigmergy. Traditional approach to capture the foraging dynamics relies on fine-tuning phenomenological rules for pheromone deposition, chemotaxis, evaporation, and behavioral switching after reaching the food source. Here, we show that stigmergy emerges from an infinite-horizon stochastic optimal control problem involving outbound foragers traveling from the nest to the food source and returning agents traveling from the food source to the nest. Pheromone dynamics along a trail emerge from the forward propagating Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, with the Bellman discount rate setting the rate of pheromone evaporation. Using this mapping, we identify the conditions under which trail feedback suppresses exploration or leads to the exploitation of established trails. For ants exploring multiple trails, we also find flux-potential relations, analogous to Ohm's law, with ant flux and inverse of squared value field playing the roles of current and resistance on the network. Our model captures collective behavior observed in the classic double-bridge experiments: trail selection on identical routes through a symmetry-breaking instability, selection of the shorter bridge, and bistability in the trail-length ratio that can leave ants transiently committed to the longer route. Our formulation places collective foraging in the broader framework of stochastic optimal control, while simultaneously providing an unifying picture on their emergent behavior consistent with experimental observations.

papers.title: Computational performance versus numerical accuracy in the acoustic terms of weakly-compressible SPH
papers.summary: Accurate computation of the acoustic terms in weakly-compressible SPH, including the equation of state, its inverse, and the evaluation of the local speed of sound, is essential to ensure energy conservation, robust solid boundary conditions, and correct open boundary behavior. In the classic Cole's equation of state, using values of the polytropic constant $γ\ne 1$ can lead to significant precision loss, particularly when computations are performed in single precision, as is common in GPU implementations. We extend here our previous results on the optimal choice of state variable by introducing a new higher-precision form for all three acoustic terms, denoted \texttt{explog}, and assess its numerical accuracy and computational performance across a variety of devices and test cases. We find that the new form evaluates the acoustic terms with a maximum ULP of~2 for arguments less than $0.125$, and has higher errors in less than 1\% of the arguments larger than the threshold. Combined with a rewritten expression of the pressure at solid boundary particles in the ``dummy'' model, it provides consistently more accurate results, maintaining deviations from the reference pressure profile to below 2\%, even in presence of a rough bottom terrain. Computationally, the new formulation is also faster than the naive one on GPU, and only marginally slower on CPU.

papers.title: Inducing cooperative dynamics in an inhomogeneous many-emitter ensemble with a pulse sequence
papers.summary: Driving a many-particle quantum system with an appropriately tuned external field can give rise to features in its nonequilibrium dynamics that are absent in the equilibrium counterpart. Cooperative dynamics in a dense ensemble of quantum emitters manifested through superradiance, a burst in the emission intensity as a function of time, is typically suppressed by spectral disparities among emitters in the ensemble. We demonstrate the enhancement of cooperative dynamics in a spectrally inhomogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters when it is driven by a periodic pulse sequence. Using both a semi-analytical mean-field solution and a digital quantum simulation, we examine the coherence of the pulse-driven ensemble and the intensity of the emitted radiation as a function of the spectral disparity in the ensemble, as a function of time, the number of atoms in the system, and as a function of the inter-pulse delay. We identify clear signatures of the enhanced cooperative dynamics for the pulse-driven inhomogeneous ensemble when dephasing in the dynamics of the ensemble is suppressed by a sufficient number of pulses during the individual emitter lifetime. These results demonstrate a post-fabrication tuning knob based on externally applied control fields for the dynamics of the many-emitter ensemble.
